UDP (User Datagram Protocol, RFC 768) is the other transport layer option: a much simpler variant than TCP.

  • It is not connection-oriented: there is no handshake and no state.
  • Error detection is optional.
  • It does no flow control or congestion control.
  • It does not sequence packets.

In exchange it is an agile protocol: useful for frequent, continuous questions, where setting up a connection for each one would be pure cost.
With UDP, the first message sent already carries the data.

The size of a header reflects the protocol's services, and UDP's is minimal: four 16-bit fields, 8 bytes in total.

  • Source port and destination port: as in TCP, they identify the application on each host.
  • UDP Total Length: the total length of the datagram, in octets.
  • Checksum: optional.

The data field follows.
Eight bytes versus TCP's twenty (at minimum).
There is no sequence number, no ACK, no flags, no window: UDP has nothing to number, acknowledge, or negotiate.

Compared with the TCP header, UDP's keeps only the ports and the checksum (and adds its length field). Each missing field is a service UDP does not provide:

  • No sequence or ACK: no acknowledgments, retransmissions, or reordering.
  • No SYN and FIN flags: no connection to open or close.
  • No Window: no flow control.
  • No options: nothing to negotiate.
Fewer fields, fewer services… and less work per message.
Highlighted, the only things TCP and UDP have in common: ports and checksum. Everything left faded does not exist in UDP.

UDP provides services similar to IP's:

  • Not connection-oriented: it keeps no state.
  • Unreliable: it sends no notifications on drops and does not reorder.
  • It does no flow control.

On top of that it adds only two things:

  • Source port and destination port, to identify services.
  • Checksum of the data part, optional.
UDP carries the IP datagram to the right application, and little more.
That is why it is chosen for non-critical applications, which need neither flow control nor error control.
Request and response: DNS and NTP

UDP is preferred for simple request-and-response processes:

  • DNS: a client's query to its name server goes over UDP because it is agile; the server is usually nearby and can be trusted without establishing a connection.
  • NTP: a client synchronizes its clock with an NTP server; it is useful, for example, to be able to compare logs.

As with TCP, services listen on well-known ports.
One question, one answer: opening and closing a connection would cost more than the exchange itself.

TCP is point-to-point: to reach several destinations, a connection would have to be established with each one. If we want to send a message to more than one, we have to use UDP:

  • Multicast and broadcast: broadcasts go over UDP.
  • Audio and video streaming.

There are no connections to maintain and no acknowledgments to wait for from each receiver.
A UDP datagram can have many recipients; a TCP connection, only two endpoints.

The destination system receives a datagram with no prior connection. It checks the destination port against the ports active at that moment:

  • If it matches none of the active ones, it sends an ICMP "destination unreachable".
  • If it matches and there is room in the buffer, it queues it.
  • If it matches but there is no room, it drops it without sending an error message.
The only notice that can come back is the inactive-port one, and ICMP sends it. Dropping for lack of room is silent.

The UDP checksum is optional and is its only error control. Since the header carries little information, a pseudo-header is added to compute it, built from information of another layer: the source and destination IP addresses, the protocol identifier, and the UDP length.

The checksum is computed over the pseudo-header, UDP header, and data. The receiver rebuilds all of that, computes the checksum, and compares it with the one it received.
It is detection, not recovery: UDP has no means to request a retransmission.
With a dotted border, the pseudo-header that each endpoint builds for the computation. Below, the UDP header and the data.

• UDP: connectionless, unreliable transport, with no flow control or congestion control, no sequencing.
  • 8-byte header: ports, length, and optional checksum.
  • Preferred for request and response (DNS, NTP), multicast and broadcast, and streaming.
  • Inactive port → ICMP destination unreachable; no room in the buffer → silent drop.
  • The checksum is computed with a pseudo-header.

With TCP and UDP, the transport layer is complete. The next unit returns to the data link layer, but in WAN networks, and starts with HDLC.
TCP: connection, acknowledgments, flow control and congestion control. UDP: ports, an optional checksum, and nothing else. The application chooses which suits it.
How large is the UDP header?
There are four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, total length, and checksum.
A UDP datagram arrives at a port where no application is active. What does the destination host do?
If the destination port matches no active one, it replies with ICMP. Silent dropping happens when the port is active but there is no room in the buffer.
Why does a DNS query go over UDP?
Because it is a simple request-and-response exchange, and UDP is agile
For one question and one answer, it is not worth establishing and releasing a connection.
Which of these services does UDP offer?
UDP adds to IP the source and destination ports and an optional checksum; it does not acknowledge, reorder, or control flow.
